I have never played a game where it felt worse to try to stumble through level maps, because they are absolutely crammed full of tiles that block movement, or sight, or both. The number of these blocking tiles would literally need to be decreased by a factor of two or three to be acceptable. The map generation process doesn't verify the inside of structures it generates connect to the outside. It doesn't even make sure the player isn't trapped in one of these inaccessible spaces when they enter a level. Awful, low contrast color choices make it hard to tell apart tiles from actors or tiles from other tiles. And that's before the screen gets smeared with blood and gunk and slime. review_text: Was incredibly fun to play at first. Compelling setting and excellent early game this has the bones of something that can be truly great. In addition, the discourse and politics surrounding this game even if I can agree with or at least respect the idea of much of the premises of it is built on, it has undeniably has gotten out of hand and wildly toxic to a shocking extent. If you are looking for a game that scratches the same itch, Tales of Maj'Eyal does a much better job in my opinion with a much nicer community.

review_text: The game is pretty fun when you are just starting out and discovering everything. It's also pretty unique and tries something that is the game industry is really lacking right now. I'd recommend it if the devs were trying to improve it, but that does not seem to be the case, so I'll judge it as a finished product. For something that calls itself a "immersive detective simulator", this game isn't immersive at all. The worst offender is probably the complete lack of consequences for player actions. You can break into a guy's house, knock out his wife in front of him, open his safe, steal all his stuff, go out the front door and run away for like 10 to 20 seconds, then come back, knock on his door, ask him to come in and he's like "Of course, make yourself at home :)". All your crimes are pardoned and you don't even have to return the $20k diamonds you stolen right in front of him and 2 cameras. Because of this, if you want money to mean anything, you pretty much need to make it a house rule not to steal anything. The NPCs really feel like lifeless robots. review_text: When I boot up a fantasy story or a game on that genre, I expect characters with different classes (swordsman, thief, mage...) to represent different backgrounds, upbringings and/or moral choices. A mage doesn't necessarily have to be a smart person, but, he has to have come from a mentor (or some tough self-learning) that leaned him towards certain life goals involving knowledge, regardless to whether he feels connected to these goals or not. When I see a werewolf character, I expect him to struggle with issues like self control, self worth... or at least address them in some way due to their inevitable messy nature. Wildermyth, however, doesn't tackle issues like that in any way. Your characters already start as warrior, archer and mage (the only 3 classes of the game) without being tied to anything, and they can transform themselves into wolves, skeletons and elemental forms without any changes in their goals or how society views them whatsoever. It's a shame, because I really like the premise of this game design, but in the end, the lack of worldbuilding being tied to what each class (and transformatiom) can do turned my experience into a big pile of blankness. review_text: Mixed on this one. Based on the reviews I had really high expectations. The game is a collection of stories and events. My main issue with the game is that the writing is too basic (children's book level + AI generated). There is no grand narrative. The mini stories and events and their random nature don't enrich the main content. Characters form relations and make choices but non of it really matters. Mom died? Oh well. Dad died? Good riddance. Made a pact and am turning into a crow? No one notices. Fell in love with a water elemental? Thank goodness we'll never see him again. Combat elements are okay. The main innovation here is the mage class which attunes to objects and casts spells based on what objects are attuned. Warrior and rogue class are standard. Character leveling is random and not influenced by your play style.
